t: 3472. Longest Palindromic Subsequence After at Most K Operations
o: Each operation shifts one character by one step around the cyclic alphabet, so making s[i] and s[j] equal costs the circular distance d = min(|a−b|, 26−|a−b|). With n, k ≤ 200 we can afford the classic interval DP augmented with a budget dimension: dp[i][j][b] = longest palindromic subsequence within s[i..j] using at most b operations.
k: Wrap-around distance between letters a and b is min(|a−b|, 26−|a−b|) — each unit costs one operation.
Interval DP: either drop s[i], drop s[j], or pay d to pair them and recurse on the inside.
Budget dimension b ranges over 0..k, giving O(n²k) states — about 8 million, comfortably fast.

a.n: Approach 1: Interval DP with operation budget
a.i: dp[i][j][b] considers the substring s[i..j] with budget b. Skipping either endpoint preserves the subsequence structure; pairing endpoints converts them to a common letter at cost d and adds 2 to the answer from the inner interval. Filling by increasing interval length yields the answer dp[0][n-1][k].
s: Base case: dp[i][i][b] = 1 for all budgets.
For lengths 2..n and each start i, compute dp[i][j][b] = max(dp[i+1][j][b], dp[i][j-1][b], and if b ≥ d, 2 + dp[i+1][j-1][b-d]).
a.t: O(n²·k) — three nested loops over interval, position, and budget

w: This is the standard LPS interval DP plus one extra dimension; recognizing the wrap-around cost function is the key observation ('z'→'a' costs 1, not 25). Verify examples: "abced", k=2 → pair (b,e) cost 3? No — optimal pairs c with c and e shifted to c, giving 3. Pitfall: when the interval has length 2, the inner dp is 0, not dp[i+1][j-1] out of bounds. Memory can be halved by keeping only two interval lengths if needed. Follow-up: reconstruct the actual operations, or handle k up to 1e9 (then budget saturates at 26·n/2 effectively).
